en: Remembering is a form of practice
Trying to recall an idea can strengthen later memory.
Rereading makes material familiar. Retrieval asks you to reconstruct it without looking; checking afterward helps correct mistakes.
Close a card, explain it in one sentence, then compare your explanation with the original.
Test your memory before reaching for the answer.
Which activity uses retrieval practice?
Reading the same paragraph again
Explaining it with the page closed
Highlighting every line
Retrieval means bringing information back from memory.
Small sessions can outlast one marathon
Spaced practice distributes learning across time.
Returning after a gap can support lasting memory. Useful spacing depends on the material and how long you want to remember it.
Revisit an idea tomorrow and later in the week instead of reading it five times immediately.
Leave a gap, then recall again.
Which schedule uses spaced practice?
Short sessions on different days
Five rereads in one sitting
One uninterrupted all-night session
Spacing separates learning sessions rather than concentrating them together.
Your favourite explanation needs a challenger
Confirmation bias favours evidence that supports an existing belief.
Searching only for agreement can make a weak belief feel well supported. Contrary evidence deserves a fair test too.
You believe a product is excellent and read only positive reviews, ignoring recurring complaints.
Ask what evidence would change your mind.
Which action helps challenge confirmation bias?
Reading only agreeing opinions
Counting repeated claims as independent proof
Examining credible evidence against your view
A fair search includes information that could contradict your belief.
The first number can set the frame
Anchoring occurs when an initial value influences a later judgement.
An early number can pull an estimate toward it even when it is a poor reference. Independent comparisons help.
An expensive first offer makes a slightly cheaper second offer feel like a bargain, despite lower prices elsewhere.
Form your own estimate before seeing someone else's.
Why can the first price affect later judgements?
It proves fair value
It becomes a mental reference point
It guarantees quality
An anchor influences comparison without establishing the right value.
Easy to remember does not mean common
The availability heuristic judges frequency using examples that come readily to mind.
Vivid or recent events are easier to recall. That ease can distort estimates of how often something happens.
After several dramatic news reports, a rare event may feel more common than the statistics suggest.
Check the base rate as well as the memorable story.
What can make an event seem unusually common?
A vivid example that is easy to recall
Its name being difficult to pronounce
The absence of any information
Memorable examples can dominate judgement without representing typical frequency.
Behaviour has a situation behind it
Attribution bias can overemphasise personality and underweight circumstances.
We often know less about another person's pressures than our own. One action is weak evidence of a permanent trait.
A late colleague seems careless until you learn their train was cancelled.
Look for a situational explanation before labelling someone.
What information could improve your judgement of a late colleague?
A harsher personality label
Your first impression alone
The circumstances of their journey
Situational information can reveal causes that a personality judgement misses.
Negative reinforcement is not punishment
Reinforcement increases a behaviour; punishment aims to decrease it.
In negative reinforcement, an unpleasant stimulus is removed after an action. Negative describes removal, not a bad outcome.
A seat-belt warning stops when you buckle up, encouraging the action.
Ask whether the behaviour increases or decreases.
A warning sound stops when a seat belt is fastened. What is this?
Punishment
Negative reinforcement
Removing every consequence
Removing the unpleasant sound encourages fastening the seat belt.
Order matters before explanation
Chronology establishes when events happened relative to one another.
A timeline can rule out impossible explanations: a cause must precede its effect. Sequence alone still does not prove causation.
A policy introduced after a protest cannot explain why that protest began.
Put the events in order before connecting them.
What does a timeline establish by itself?
The order of events
The single cause of every event
Everyone's motives
Chronology gives sequence; causal explanations need additional evidence.
Read the document's world, too
Historical context concerns the conditions in which a source was created.
Audience, institutions, available knowledge and social pressures shape what a document means.
A public speech and a private letter by the same person may use different language for different audiences.
Ask who could hear or read these words at the time.
Which detail helps contextualise a speech?
Only its font
Its intended audience and circumstances
Your preferred modern opinion
The original setting helps explain how and why a source was produced.
Agreement is stronger when sources are independent
Corroboration compares evidence from more than one source.
Two accounts repeating one earlier report are not two independent witnesses. Differences can be informative as well as agreement.
Compare a diary, a dated photograph and an official record rather than three copies of one article.
Trace where each account obtained its information.
Which evidence offers stronger independent corroboration?
Three copied articles
One repeated rumour
Separate records made by different observers
Independent origins matter more than the number of repetitions.
Do not lend the past tomorrow's knowledge
An anachronism places something in the wrong historical time.
Using later technology or information to explain earlier decisions can distort what people could actually know or do.
Judging an old voyage as if its crew had satellite forecasts assigns them tools they never possessed.
Separate knowledge available then from knowledge available now.
Which judgement contains an anachronism?
Expecting an eighteenth-century crew to use satellite forecasts
Checking the voyage date
Comparing contemporary ship logs
Satellite forecasting belongs to a later period.
Memory is evidence with a perspective
Oral history records people's recollections and interpretations of the past.
Interviews preserve experiences that documents may omit. Memory and later context can reshape an account, so comparison remains important.
A worker's interview adds daily experience to a factory's official records.
Value the testimony while checking dates and other evidence.
Why compare an interview with other sources?
Spoken evidence is always false
Memory can change and perspective matters
Official records are always complete
An interview is valuable evidence, but neither memory nor documents are flawless.
An object's location is part of its story
Archaeological context links a find to its position and associated material.
An object removed without recording its surroundings loses evidence about use, date and relationships.
A coin found in a documented floor layer says more than a coin with no recorded origin.
Ask where a find came from, not only what it is.
What adds important meaning to an artefact?
Its price alone
A polished appearance
Its recorded location and associations
Context connects an object to the wider evidence of a site.

sourceName: UCLA · National Center for History in the Schools
en: Historical periods are useful boundaries
Periodisation divides the past into named eras for analysis.
The boundaries highlight some changes and hide others. A transition can happen at different times in different places.
A political revolution may transform government immediately while farming habits change much more slowly.
Ask what changed at the boundary and for whom.
Why might one period boundary not fit every region?
Changes occurred at different times
All dates are meaningless
Every society changed identically
Periods are analytical tools rather than universal simultaneous switches.
A conclusion needs a route
A deductive argument is valid when true premises would guarantee its conclusion.
Validity concerns the connection between claims, not whether the premises are actually true.
All dragons breathe fire; Mira is a dragon; therefore Mira breathes fire. The structure works even with fictional premises.
Check the logical connection separately from the facts.
Can a valid argument have false premises?
No, validity makes every premise true
Yes, validity concerns the structure
Only if it has no conclusion
Validity tests whether the conclusion follows if the premises are true.
Good structure also needs true starting points
A sound deductive argument is valid and has true premises.
A tidy logical chain can still mislead if it begins with a false claim. Soundness requires both parts.
A claim about every customer cannot be established using an unverified premise about all people.
Ask: does it follow, and are its starting claims true?
What makes a deductive argument sound?
An impressive speaker
A true conclusion alone
Valid structure and true premises
Both validity and true premises are required.
Required does not mean enough
A necessary condition must be present; a sufficient condition guarantees the result.
An ingredient can be indispensable without producing an outcome on its own. Confusing these roles causes weak arguments.
A charged battery is necessary for this battery-powered torch to work, but a broken bulb can still prevent light.
Ask whether a condition is required, enough, or both.
Why is a charged battery not sufficient in this example?
The bulb may also be broken
Batteries never supply energy
The torch needs no other parts
Other required conditions can still be missing.
One ethical lens looks at outcomes
Consequentialism evaluates actions by their consequences.
Different consequentialist theories disagree about which outcomes matter. Predictions and who is affected become central questions.
Comparing two policies by the harm each prevents uses an outcome-focused lens.
Identify whose outcomes are counted and what is uncertain.
Which question is most directly consequentialist?
Does this follow a duty regardless of results?
What outcomes will this action produce?
Who spoke first?
Consequentialism places consequences at the centre of moral evaluation.
Another ethical lens asks about duties
Deontological ethics gives duties or constraints a central role.
An attractive outcome does not automatically justify every method. Different theories explain duties and conflicts differently.
Refusing to deceive a customer despite a possible sale can reflect a duty-based judgement.
Ask which principle the action respects or violates.
Which consideration is central to a duty-based judgement?
Only sales revenue
Only popularity
Whether the action respects a moral duty
Deontology does not assess actions solely by their consequences.
Ethics can ask who you are becoming
Virtue ethics emphasises character and cultivated qualities.
Instead of examining only rules or outcomes, it asks how judgement and habits express qualities such as honesty and courage.
Practising honest feedback builds a disposition, not just a record of isolated compliant acts.
What kind of character does this repeated action cultivate?
Which question reflects virtue ethics?
What kind of person does this habit help me become?
What is the cheapest option?
Can every rule be ignored?
Virtue ethics focuses on character and practical judgement.
Confidence is not the same as knowledge
Epistemology studies knowledge, justification and belief.
Feeling certain does not establish that a belief is true or well supported. Philosophers investigate what distinguishes knowledge from a lucky guess.
Guessing tomorrow's weather correctly once does not show that your method was reliable.
Separate the claim from your reasons for believing it.
Why does one correct guess not establish a reliable method?
Correct answers are never useful
It could have been correct by luck
Confidence always proves truth
Accuracy in one case does not by itself establish justification or reliability.
Two symbols can represent a whole world
Binary represents numbers using digits 0 and 1.
Each position has a power-of-two value. Agreed encodings let patterns of bits represent text, images and other data.
Binary 101 means 4 + 0 + 1, so it represents decimal 5.
Distinguish the bit pattern from the encoding used to interpret it.
What decimal number does binary 101 represent?
Its positions represent four, two and one; 1×4 + 0×2 + 1×1 = 5.
Encryption protects the contents
Encryption transforms readable data into ciphertext using an algorithm and key.
An authorised recipient uses the appropriate key to recover the message. Protection also depends on implementation and key handling.
An encrypted message can travel across a network without exposing its readable contents to every intermediary.
Ask who can access the keys, not only whether encryption is mentioned.
What is the main purpose of encryption?
Protecting readable content from unauthorised access
Making every file smaller
Proving every message is truthful
Encryption protects confidentiality; it does not make a claim true.
A hash is a fingerprint, not a locked box
A cryptographic hash maps data to a fixed-length digest.
It is designed to resist recovering the input and finding matching digests for different inputs. Hashing is not reversible encryption.
Comparing a downloaded file's hash with a trusted published hash can help detect a change.
Use a trusted reference; a matching hash alone does not identify a trustworthy publisher.
How does hashing differ from encryption?
Hashing always preserves the original message
A hash is not intended to be decrypted
Hashes guarantee all downloads are safe
Hashing produces a digest rather than reversible ciphertext.
Learning can begin with labelled examples
Supervised learning learns relationships between inputs and known target labels.
Training examples guide a model toward predictions for new inputs. The usefulness of those predictions depends on data and evaluation.
A spam classifier learns from emails labelled spam or not spam.
Ask how the labels were created and whether new cases resemble the training data.
Which dataset supports supervised learning?
Emails with no targets or labels
Only a random list of numbers
Emails paired with spam or not-spam labels
Known target labels provide the learning signal.
Memorising examples is not generalising
Overfitting occurs when a model fits training data but performs poorly on new data.
A model may learn accidental details rather than useful patterns. Evaluation on separate data helps expose the problem.
A classifier recognises its training photos perfectly but fails on new photographs.
Judge performance on examples the model did not train on.
Which result suggests overfitting?
Excellent training results and poor new-data results
Similar good results on training and new data
No training examples at all
The gap suggests the model learned training-specific details.
A wide road can still have a long journey
Bandwidth describes capacity; latency describes delay.
More capacity can move more data at once, but it does not automatically reduce the time for a request to travel and return.
A video call can feel delayed despite a connection advertised with a high download rate.
Ask about response time as well as transfer capacity.
What does high bandwidth guarantee by itself?
Zero delay
Greater data-transfer capacity, not necessarily lower latency
Instant responses from every server
Capacity and delay describe different aspects of a connection.
History makes changes easier to manage
Version control records changes so earlier states can be compared or recovered.
A useful history explains what changed and supports collaboration. It is more structured than a folder of files named final-final.
A team can identify which edit introduced a problem and inspect the previous working version.
Record meaningful changes with clear explanations.
What is a key benefit of version control?
It prevents every possible bug
It removes the need to review changes
It preserves a traceable change history
Recorded versions make comparison and recovery possible.
Some costs move with output
Variable costs change with activity; total fixed costs stay stable within a relevant range.
Fixed does not mean permanent. Rent may stay unchanged for a month while packaging rises with every extra order.
Selling one more meal needs extra ingredients but may not change this month's rent.
Separate costs per extra unit from costs of keeping the operation open.
Which cost is usually variable in this example?
Ingredients for one more meal
The unchanged monthly rent
A fixed monthly licence fee
Ingredients increase when another meal is produced.
Profit is not cash in the bank
Profit and cash flow measure different things.
A recorded sale may create profit before the customer pays. Cash timing determines whether bills can be paid now.
A profitable business with unpaid invoices can still struggle to cover wages this week.
Track when money arrives and leaves, not only reported profit.
Why can a profitable firm be short of cash?
Profit guarantees immediate payment
Customers may not have paid yet
Cash and profit are identical
Recorded earnings and actual receipts can occur at different times.
Break-even asks how many sales cover the basics
Break-even occurs when total revenue equals total costs.
In a simple single-product model, fixed costs divided by contribution per unit gives the units needed to break even.
With fixed costs of €100 and €5 contribution per sale, 20 sales cover those fixed costs.
Check the assumptions behind the calculation.
How many sales cover €100 fixed costs at €5 contribution each?
100 divided by 5 equals 20, under the stated assumptions.
A sale has to help pay the fixed costs
Contribution per unit is selling price minus variable cost per unit.
That remainder contributes toward fixed costs and then profit. It is not automatically the final profit on the sale.
A €10 item with €6 variable cost contributes €4 before fixed costs are covered.
Calculate what one extra sale actually contributes.
What is the contribution of a €10 sale with €6 variable cost?
Subtract variable cost from the selling price: 10 − 6 = 4.
Start with the customer's problem
A value proposition explains a useful benefit for a particular customer.
Features describe a product; value explains why someone would choose it. Testing the problem comes before assuming demand.
A booking tool matters to a busy customer because it reduces coordination, not merely because it has many buttons.
Ask whom it helps and which difficulty it removes.
Which statement communicates customer value?
Our app has 20 screens
Book an appointment without repeated phone calls
We used a fashionable programming language
The statement connects the offering to a concrete customer benefit.

sourceName: OECD · The Digital Transformation of SMEs
en: A network can become more useful as it grows
A network effect occurs when participation changes value for other users.
A messaging service can become more useful when the people you need join it. More users do not improve every product automatically.
A chat app used by all your friends is easier to use for communication than an isolated alternative.
Identify who benefits from each additional participant.
Which example shows a network effect?
A product getting heavier
A price increasing with no new users
A messaging app becoming useful as friends join
Other participants add opportunities to communicate.
The slowest stage can set the pace
A bottleneck constrains the throughput of a process.
Speeding up a stage that already has spare capacity may not increase final output. The limiting stage deserves attention.
A café can prepare 30 orders an hour but take payment for only 15; faster preparation alone will not fix the queue.
Find the limiting step before improving the busiest-looking step.
What limits output in this café example?
Payment capacity
The colour of the cups
Preparation capacity of 30 orders
Only 15 payments an hour can pass through the limiting stage.
Stability requires constant adjustment
Homeostasis maintains internal conditions within workable ranges.
Negative feedback counters a deviation rather than keeping the body perfectly unchanged.
When body temperature rises, sweating can help release heat and oppose the increase.
Look for the variable, the sensor and the corrective response.
Which example illustrates negative feedback?
A change reinforcing itself indefinitely
Sweating opposing a rise in temperature
A body never responding to change
The response works against the deviation.
Breathing creates an exchange surface
Oxygen and carbon dioxide diffuse across the thin alveolar-capillary barrier.
Differences in partial pressure drive gases in opposite directions between air and blood.
Oxygen passes from alveolar air into blood while carbon dioxide moves from blood toward the air to be exhaled.
Separate moving air from exchanging gases.
Where does most lung gas exchange occur?
In the throat
Only in the nose
Across the alveolar-capillary barrier
The thin barrier allows diffusion between alveolar air and blood.
Cells need usable energy, not just fuel
ATP helps couple energy-releasing processes to cellular work.
Cells continually produce and use ATP. It is an energy-transfer molecule rather than a large long-term fuel store.
Muscle contraction uses ATP while metabolism replenishes it from available fuels.
Distinguish stored fuel from the molecule that helps power immediate work.
What is an important role of ATP?
Coupling energy supply to cellular work
Storing all body fat permanently
Replacing every nutrient
ATP participates in transferring usable energy to cellular processes.
A chemical message needs a receiver
Hormones act on target cells with suitable receptors.
A hormone may circulate widely, but cells respond according to their receptors and signalling machinery.
A signal in the blood does not make every tissue perform the same action.
Ask which cells can receive the message.
Why do only some cells respond to a hormone?
Blood never reaches other cells
They have the relevant receptors
All hormones affect every cell identically
Target-cell receptors help determine the response.
Movement needs a connection
Tendons transmit force from muscle to bone.
Muscles generate tension; connective tissue transfers it to the skeleton. Tendons and ligaments serve different main connections.
A contracting calf muscle pulls through the Achilles tendon to move the heel.
Distinguish muscle-to-bone from bone-to-bone connections.
What is the main connection made by a tendon?
Bone to bone
Nerve to skin
Muscle to bone
Tendons connect muscle and bone; ligaments commonly connect bones.
Bone is living tissue
Bone is continually maintained through formation and resorption.
Remodelling renews tissue and responds to mechanical demands and biological signals. Bone is not an inert support beam.
The skeleton keeps changing even after a person has reached adult height.
Think of bone as an active tissue, not a fixed object.
Which statement describes adult bone?
It continues to remodel
It becomes completely inactive
It contains no living cells
Bone formation and resorption continue throughout adult life.
The body keeps time
Circadian rhythms organise many processes on an approximately 24-hour cycle.
Internal clocks interact with cues such as light. Timing affects patterns of sleepiness and alertness.
Crossing time zones can put the local light-dark cycle out of step with an internal clock.
Notice both how long and when you sleep.
What can influence the timing of circadian rhythms?
Only the size of a clock
Light-dark cues
A complete absence of internal rhythms
Light is an important cue for aligning internal timing with the environment.
The surface is moving beneath us
Plate tectonics describes motion of Earth's lithospheric plates.
Plates separate, converge or slide past one another. Their boundaries help explain patterns of earthquakes, volcanoes and mountain building.
A band of earthquakes can trace the boundary between moving plates.
Look at boundaries when interpreting geological patterns.
Why are many earthquakes concentrated in bands?
Every location has identical conditions
Maps cause earthquakes
Many occur near moving plate boundaries
Plate interaction concentrates many geological processes along boundaries.
A river connects a whole landscape
A watershed is the area that drains toward a shared outlet.
Water and material from upstream can affect places downstream. Watershed boundaries often follow high ground, not political borders.
Rain on different sides of a ridge may flow into different rivers.
Trace the drainage area, not just the visible river.
What commonly separates neighbouring watersheds?
A ridge or other drainage divide
Every national border
The river's colour
Higher ground can direct water toward different outlets.
A city can hold extra heat
Urban heat islands are urban areas warmer than nearby surroundings.
Surfaces, buildings, reduced vegetation and human activity influence heat storage and release. Conditions vary within a city.
A paved area without shade may remain warmer than a nearby tree-covered space.
Compare land cover when comparing local temperatures.
Which feature can contribute to an urban heat island?
More shade from trees
Extensive heat-absorbing surfaces and little vegetation
Identical land cover everywhere
The built environment changes how heat is absorbed and released.
One cold day does not describe a climate
Weather is short-term atmospheric conditions; climate describes long-term patterns.
Individual days vary around broader distributions. A trend requires observations over longer periods.
A rainy holiday tells you about those days, not the destination's entire climate.
Match the timescale of the evidence to the question.
Which evidence better describes climate?
One afternoon's temperature
A single storm photograph
Long-term temperature and rainfall patterns
Climate concerns long-term characteristics rather than one event.
Scale decides how much fits on a map
A map scale relates distance on the map to distance on the ground.
At 1:100,000, one unit on the map represents 100,000 of the same units on the ground.
At that scale, 1 centimetre represents 1 kilometre.
Check scale before estimating distance or expecting detail.
At 1:100,000, what does 1 cm represent?
1 km
100 km
1 metre
100,000 centimetres equals 1 kilometre.
A mountain can divide wet and dry
A rain shadow can form on the downwind side of a mountain range.
Air rising over mountains cools and may lose moisture as precipitation. Descending air on the other side can be warmer and drier.
Two nearby valleys can have different rainfall because a mountain separates their airflow.
Consider prevailing wind and terrain together.
Which side is commonly drier in a rain-shadow pattern?
The windward rising-air side
The downwind descending-air side
Both sides must be identical
Descending air after moisture loss can create a drier downwind region.
An average can hide where people live
Population density divides population by land area.
A regional average does not reveal settlement patterns within it. People may be concentrated in a few cities.
An area with 10,000 people across 100 km² has average density 100 people per km², even if most live in one town.
Ask about distribution as well as the average.
What is the average density in this example?
10 people per km²
1,000 people per km²
100 people per km²
10,000 divided by 100 equals 100; the average can still hide concentration.
Familiar is not automatically universal
Ethnocentrism judges another culture mainly by one's own cultural standards.
Treating familiar practices as the only normal ones can block understanding of different meanings.
You assume a different greeting is disrespectful because it is not the greeting you learned.
Describe the difference before ranking it.
Which judgement illustrates ethnocentrism?
Their greeting is wrong because it differs from ours
What does this greeting mean here?
How did this practice develop?
The judgement uses one's own custom as the universal standard.
Understanding starts with local meaning
Cultural relativism examines practices within their cultural context.
Understanding a practice is different from endorsing everything about it. Context helps explain what people mean and value.
Before judging an unfamiliar ceremony, ask participants what its actions signify.
Seek explanation before assuming the meaning.
What does contextual understanding require?
Approving every practice automatically
Investigating what it means within that culture
Ignoring the participants
Understanding local meaning does not require automatic moral approval.
Objects carry shared meanings
Material culture includes the physical objects people create and use.
Nonmaterial culture includes ideas and values. The two interact: an object can embody a belief or social relationship.
A wedding ring is a physical object linked to ideas about commitment.
Ask both what an object does and what it represents.
Which item is an example of material culture?
A belief about loyalty
An unwritten expectation
A wedding ring
The ring is a physical object; its meaning involves nonmaterial culture.
Values and norms play different roles
Values express what a group considers important; norms guide behaviour.
A broad value can be supported by several specific expectations. Stated values and actual behaviour can differ.
Respect is a value; waiting your turn in a queue is a norm that may express it.
Separate the principle from the expected action.
Which example is a behavioural norm?
Waiting your turn in a queue
The broad ideal of fairness
The abstract importance of respect
A norm specifies expected conduct rather than only an ideal.
One society contains many cultural worlds
A subculture shares distinctive practices within a larger society.
Membership does not mean rejecting every wider social value. People can belong to several groups at once.
A professional community develops vocabulary and routines that outsiders do not immediately recognise.
Avoid treating a whole society as culturally identical.
What is a subculture?
A group with no shared practices
A distinctive cultural group within a larger society
Every member of society behaving identically
Distinctive practices can exist within a wider shared social setting.
Ideas travel and change
Cultural diffusion is the spread of practices, objects or ideas between groups.
Adoption can involve adaptation rather than exact copying. Contact, migration and communication create routes for exchange.
A food tradition travels with migrants and develops new local versions.
Trace both the route and the changes.
Which example illustrates diffusion?
An idea never leaving one group
Every tradition remaining unchanged
A food practice spreading and adapting elsewhere
Diffusion carries cultural elements across groups, often with adaptation.
Repeated actions can express belonging
Rituals are patterned actions with shared symbolic meaning.
A ritual can mark a transition or connect participants to a group. Repetition alone does not explain its meaning.
A graduation ceremony marks a change in status through familiar gestures and symbols.
Ask what the action marks and who recognises its meaning.
What distinguishes a ritual from mere repetition?
Shared symbolic meaning
Only the number of times it happens
The absence of participants
Meaning and social recognition matter, not repetition alone.
Flight is a balance of forces
Lift, weight, thrust and drag act on an aircraft.
Lift and drag are defined relative to airflow; weight acts toward Earth. A steady straight flight can have balanced forces without being stationary.
An aircraft cruising at constant velocity still has forces acting on it.
Distinguish balanced forces from an absence of forces.
What can balanced forces produce?
Only a motionless object
Constant velocity in a straight line
Automatic acceleration
Zero net force permits constant velocity; it does not require zero speed.
The wing's angle is relative to the airflow
Angle of attack is the angle between the wing chord and relative airflow.
It is different from the aircraft's pitch attitude relative to the horizon. A changing flight path changes the relationship.
The same nose attitude can correspond to different angles of attack during different flight paths.
Name the reference line before comparing angles.
What reference defines angle of attack?
Only the horizon
The airport runway
The relative airflow and wing chord
Angle of attack is referenced to airflow, not simply the horizon.
A stall is an airflow problem
An aerodynamic stall occurs when a wing exceeds its critical angle of attack.
Flow separation reduces lift capability. A stall is not the same as an engine stopping and is not defined by one universal speed.
Different loading or manoeuvres can change the airspeed at which a wing reaches its critical angle.
Separate engine condition, airspeed and angle of attack.
What defines an aerodynamic stall?
Exceeding the critical angle of attack
Any engine stopping
Passing a universal speed for all aircraft
The critical angle of attack is central to the stall condition.
Moving through air has a cost
Drag is an aerodynamic force opposing motion relative to the air.
Shape, speed and flow conditions affect drag. Drag associated with producing lift is one part of the total.
Changing an aircraft's configuration can change drag even when the aircraft stays the same size.
Ask which source of drag changes in the situation.
Which statement about drag is correct?
Only engines generate it
Many aircraft surfaces contribute to it
It never changes with airflow
Drag comes from interaction between the aircraft and air.
A checklist supports memory
A checklist helps verify important actions in a repeatable way.
Its usefulness depends on design, timing and disciplined use. It supports understanding rather than replacing it.
A cross-check can catch an omitted step that felt familiar enough to remember.
Treat verification as an action, not a ritual of reading words.
What is a sensible role for a checklist?
Replace all system knowledge
Guarantee nobody can make an error
Support reliable verification of important actions
Checklists reduce reliance on memory but still require appropriate use.
Safety improves when resources work together
Resource management coordinates people, information and available tools.
Clear communication and decisions help a team use knowledge distributed across its members and supporting services.
A team member voices a concern early, allowing the others to check an assumption before it becomes a problem.
Make concerns clear and invite useful information.
Which action supports resource management?
Communicating a relevant concern clearly
Hiding uncertainty to appear confident
Ignoring supporting information
Useful information must reach the people making the decision.
Hotter air can change performance
Density altitude expresses air density as an equivalent altitude in a standard atmosphere.
Higher density altitude means less dense air. This can reduce aircraft performance; the effect depends on the aircraft and conditions.
A hot day can make an airport perform like a higher-elevation location than its actual elevation suggests.
Distinguish airport elevation from the density of the air.
What does higher density altitude mean?
Denser air
Less dense air
An airport physically moving uphill
Density altitude describes the air, not a change in the airport's ground elevation.
